paths.title: Beginner
paths.description: Start with queries, tools, permissions, sessions, and the first offline tests.
paths.outcome: Build confidence with the SDK's core concepts and inspect a complete test result.

paths.title: Application Developer
paths.description: Build a usable agent application with tools, streaming, approvals, safety, and integrations.
paths.outcome: Connect an agent to a browser and server, then examine application checks and deployment patterns.

paths.title: Advanced Harness
paths.description: Study orchestration, durable sessions, evaluation, security, and verified team handoffs.
paths.outcome: Design and evaluate a production-style agent harness before tackling the final team capstone.

questions.prompt: What does query() return while an agent runs?

options.text: Only one final answer string
options.explanation: Lesson 1 shows intermediate system and assistant messages before the final result.

options.text: An async stream of SDK messages
options.explanation: Correct. Iterate the stream and inspect each message type.

options.text: A browser DOM element
options.explanation: The SDK produces messages; your application decides how to render them.

questions.prompt: Which message tells you the run has finished?

options.text: The system/init message
options.explanation: Initialization marks the start of a session, not completion.

options.text: The first assistant text chunk
options.explanation: Assistant text may be partial. Keep reading until the terminal result.

options.text: The final result message
options.explanation: Correct. Check the terminal result and its success or error fields.

questions.prompt: Where do you set which tools the agent may use?

options.text: In the query options
options.explanation: Correct. Configure the allowed tools in the options supplied to the run.

options.text: By editing the assistant's final text
options.explanation: Final text reports output; it cannot retroactively configure tool access.

options.text: Only in the browser CSS
options.explanation: CSS changes presentation, not the SDK's tool configuration.

questions.prompt: Why retain a session identifier?

options.text: It guarantees every future answer is correct
options.explanation: A session identifier preserves continuity, but it does not validate answer quality.

options.text: It lets a later turn continue the same conversation
options.explanation: Correct. Use the session information when resuming a conversation.

options.text: It replaces all tool permissions
options.explanation: Session continuity and permissions are separate concerns.

questions.prompt: What should you check before saying a background task finished?

options.text: That the foreground turn ended
options.explanation: The foreground turn can end while the background task keeps running.

options.text: That you saved a task ID
options.explanation: A task ID helps track work, but it is not completion evidence.

options.text: The matching terminal notification or task state
options.explanation: Correct. Match the task identity to its final state.

questions.prompt: What does context compaction aim to preserve?

options.text: The information needed for subsequent turns
options.explanation: Correct. Compare what was retained with what the next turn needs.

options.text: Every prior token unchanged
options.explanation: Compaction reduces context; it does not keep every token verbatim.

options.text: Only the latest UI colors
options.explanation: Context is about conversation and task information, not visual styling.

questions.prompt: When does a hook affect an agent run?

options.text: At its configured lifecycle event
options.explanation: Correct. Inspect which event invokes the hook and what it returns.

options.text: Only after the browser closes
options.explanation: Hooks are tied to configured agent lifecycle events.

options.text: Only when CSS changes
options.explanation: UI styling has no bearing on hook invocation.

questions.prompt: What belongs in project configuration rather than a one-off prompt?

options.text: A student's single question
options.explanation: A one-off question is input for a run, not persistent project configuration.

options.text: Settings intended to apply across project runs
options.explanation: Correct. Use project-level configuration for shared behavior.

options.text: The final text of a completed answer
options.explanation: An answer is an output, not a reusable setting.

questions.prompt: How should you confirm a hook did what you intended?

options.text: Assume registration proves behavior
options.explanation: Registration alone does not show the event fired or the return was handled.

options.text: Count the number of browser tabs
options.explanation: Browser tabs do not establish hook behavior.

options.text: Inspect the triggering event and observed outcome
options.explanation: Correct. Match the hook event to the effect in the run.

questions.prompt: What makes an MCP tool call trustworthy as completed work?

options.text: The tool name appears in a prompt
options.explanation: Mentioning a tool is not evidence that it ran.

options.text: The model says it probably worked
options.explanation: A model claim alone cannot establish the tool's result.

options.text: The tool response and resulting state support the claim
options.explanation: Correct. Inspect the actual response and relevant state.

questions.prompt: What should happen to invalid tool input?

options.text: Reject it at the appropriate validation boundary
options.explanation: Correct. Check which layer rejected the input: the tool's schema or the handler's own validation.

options.text: Report it as accepted server content
options.explanation: Invalid input must not be represented as accepted work.

options.text: Silently change it into a successful result
options.explanation: Silent success hides the validation problem from the student.

questions.prompt: Why inspect a tool's schema before calling it?

options.text: To avoid ever reading the result
options.explanation: The result still needs inspection after a call.

options.text: To supply the expected arguments and interpret the output
options.explanation: Correct. A schema defines the call contract.

options.text: To replace tool permissions
options.explanation: A schema describes inputs; it does not grant access.

questions.prompt: After a retry event, what proves the run eventually succeeded?

options.text: The retry event itself
options.explanation: A retry only records another attempt; it is not a terminal success.

options.text: The first partial assistant response
options.explanation: Partial output can precede a failure or another retry.

options.text: A final successful result after the retry
options.explanation: Correct. Follow the event sequence through its terminal result.

questions.prompt: What should a plan or task list describe?

options.text: The work and its actual progress
options.explanation: Correct. Update status from observed work rather than guesses.

options.text: Only completed work before it starts
options.explanation: Premature completion hides unfinished steps.

options.text: An unrelated sample answer
options.explanation: A plan should track this task's steps.

questions.prompt: When should a workflow ask the user a question?

options.text: For every routine implementation choice
options.explanation: Routine choices can usually be resolved from context.

options.text: When a missing decision materially changes the next step
options.explanation: Correct. Ask a focused question for the information the workflow needs.

options.text: Only after claiming the work is complete
options.explanation: A blocking clarification belongs before dependent work.

questions.prompt: What is good evidence that a delegated task is complete?

options.text: A message saying a task was assigned
options.explanation: Assignment proves delegation, not completion.

options.text: The expected output and a verified final task state
options.explanation: Correct. Match the output and status to the delegated task.

options.text: An unrelated agent's answer
options.explanation: Evidence must refer to the same task and agent work.

questions.prompt: Why identify ownership before handing off work?

options.text: To avoid inspecting the result
options.explanation: Ownership improves coordination, but verification remains necessary.

options.text: To make every agent edit the same file at once
options.explanation: Uncoordinated overlapping edits invite conflicts.

options.text: To clarify who produces and checks each deliverable
options.explanation: Correct. Clear ownership supports a reliable handoff.

questions.prompt: How should you judge the final team capstone?

options.text: Compare deliverables and verified team state with the goal
options.explanation: Correct. Review the actual artifacts and completion evidence.

options.text: Count only the number of spawned agents
options.explanation: Agent count does not show whether the goal was met.

options.text: Assume a handoff message is the finished product
options.explanation: A handoff can precede unfinished work.

questions.prompt: What controls whether an agent can perform a sensitive action?

options.text: The color of the action button
options.explanation: UI color does not grant or restrict agent permissions.

options.text: The configured permission and approval boundary
options.explanation: Correct. Inspect the policy and any required approval step.

options.text: The length of the prompt
options.explanation: Prompt length is unrelated to authorization.

questions.prompt: How should external text be treated when it tries to change the agent's instructions?

options.text: As untrusted content, not a new authority
options.explanation: Correct. Keep source content separate from governing instructions.

options.text: As an automatic override of the system prompt
options.explanation: A retrieved page cannot promote itself into higher-priority instructions.

options.text: As proof that the user approved the change
options.explanation: Untrusted text cannot establish user approval.

questions.prompt: What should a sandbox restriction be checked against?

options.text: Only the agent's confidence
options.explanation: Confidence is not evidence of an allowed operation.

options.text: The lesson title alone
options.explanation: A title cannot establish an execution boundary.

options.text: The actual operation and its configured boundary
options.explanation: Correct. Evaluate the action against the sandbox configuration.

questions.prompt: What makes an automated test a useful deployment signal?

options.text: It was launched, regardless of its result
options.explanation: A started test says nothing about pass or failure.

options.text: A checklist box was ticked
options.explanation: Self-assessment is not an automated test result.

options.text: The complete test run passed its defined checks
options.explanation: Correct. Inspect the terminal test result and scope of checks.

questions.prompt: What should you do when an SDK upgrade compatibility gate fails?

options.text: Ignore the failure and deploy
options.explanation: A failed gate needs investigation before relying on the candidate.

options.text: Inspect the failing gate and block or fix the incompatible change
options.explanation: Correct. Follow the gate evidence; the lesson's simulation is not a real deployment.

options.text: Report every gate as passed
options.explanation: Misreporting the result hides the incompatibility.

questions.prompt: What evidence distinguishes an observed deployment from a deployment plan?

options.text: A running target and successful check against it
options.explanation: Correct. Verify the actual target and behavior before claiming a live deployment.

options.text: A written command that nobody ran
options.explanation: A command in documentation is a plan, not observed deployment.

options.text: An unchecked architecture diagram
options.explanation: A diagram illustrates design, not runtime success.

visual_guides.title: Foundations
visual_guides.description: Meet the agent, model, tools and context before your first query.
visual_guides.question: Which part executes a tool, and which part decides whether it is allowed?
visual_guides.answer: The host executes the tool under its permission policy. The model can request a tool call; that request does not authorize its effect.
visual_guides.note: Runner is a conceptual execution role in this map. In this app, trace agent_lab/runtime.py (host) and agent_lab/sdk.py (SDK options and query).
visual_guides.takeaway: Connect the user request, host orchestration, model, context and tools before inspecting the output.

points.title: Agent
points.text: Instructions, behavior and goals define the task.

points.title: User input
points.text: The user supplies messages or tasks.

points.title: Tools
points.text: Host functions expose capabilities the agent can request.

points.title: Model
points.text: Claude generates responses and can propose tool calls.

points.title: Context
points.text: Conversation state and relevant information inform the run.

points.title: Runner
points.text: The host and SDK orchestrate execution.

points.title: Output
points.text: Inspect the final response or structured result.

points.title: Why it matters
points.text: These parts form a reusable structure for agent applications.

visual_guides.title: Execution flow
visual_guides.description: Trace the journey from a user request to tool results and final evidence.
visual_guides.question: Does receiving an assistant answer prove that the exercise completed successfully?
visual_guides.answer: No. Inspect the terminal result, normal stream closure and the lesson-specific host evidence. Partial text or a fluent answer can accompany a failed or interrupted run.
visual_guides.note: This is a lifecycle overview, not a strict timeline of every SDK event. Tool use may repeat or be skipped. Logs expose observable events, not private internal reasoning.
visual_guides.takeaway: Compare the map with actual messages, tool results and terminal evidence after running the exercise.

points.title: User request
points.text: A message or task enters the application.

points.title: Runner starts
points.text: The host starts SDK execution.

points.title: Agent reasoning
points.text: The model interprets the task; private reasoning is not a required visible application event.

points.title: Tool calls
points.text: The model can request tools when needed, subject to host permissions.

points.title: Tool results
points.text: Host results return to the conversation.

points.title: State update
points.text: The application updates observed context and progress.

points.title: Final response
points.text: A final answer must be distinguished from successful terminal completion.

points.title: Observability
points.text: Logs and traces help inspect what actually happened.

visual_guides.title: Multi-agent patterns
visual_guides.description: Explore delegation, explicit context and verified handoffs across agents.
visual_guides.question: Do specialist agents automatically share all context and trusted results?
visual_guides.answer: No. The application must explicitly pass context, define permissions and validate handoffs. An agent report is a claim until the host verifies its evidence.
visual_guides.note: Shared context requires explicit implementation. Delegation, tool access and result aggregation are application design choices; they are not automatically trusted shared memory.
visual_guides.takeaway: Break a larger goal into bounded roles, with explicit handoffs and a clear integration owner.

points.title: Coordinator agent
points.text: Receives the goal and manages the workflow.

points.title: Specialist agents
points.text: Each agent handles a narrow task.

points.title: Handoffs
points.text: Pass work and the evidence needed by the next role.

points.title: Shared context
points.text: Pass the information each role needs explicitly.

points.title: Tool access
points.text: Give each role the tools and permissions it needs.

points.title: Result aggregation
points.text: Combine outputs with validation and conflict handling.

points.title: Structured output
points.text: Use explicit contracts for role results.

points.title: Human review
points.text: Keep an appropriate review gate for critical steps.

visual_guides.title: Best practices
visual_guides.description: A practical design-review reference for safer, observable and testable agents.
visual_guides.question: What evidence would you request before calling an agent ready for production?
visual_guides.answer: Look for clear acceptance criteria, tested host effects and permissions, recovery behavior, useful logs, known limits and evaluation results. A diagram or checklist alone cannot establish production readiness.
visual_guides.note: Use this as a review reference. Completing a review does not certify production readiness or automatically complete a lesson.
visual_guides.takeaway: Combine clear goals, predictable tools, guarded effects, observability and ongoing evaluation.

points.title: Clear instructions
points.text: Define goals, boundaries and success criteria.

points.title: Tool design
points.text: Use predictable, validated inputs and outputs.

points.title: Guardrails
points.text: Validate risky or invalid actions at the host boundary.

points.title: Error handling
points.text: Recover deliberately when a tool or run fails.

points.title: Testing
points.text: Evaluate prompts, tools, workflows and effects.

points.title: Observability
points.text: Track events, logs and outcomes.

points.title: Cost awareness
points.text: Bound and inspect quality, latency and usage.

points.title: User experience
points.text: Return useful progress and honest final results.
